title: Evilnum
summary: Evilnum is a threat activity group that public reporting links to targeted campaigns against financial technology and online trading platforms, mostly in Europe and the Middle East. The name is used both for the actor and for tooling described in the same reports. Documented intrusion chains begin with spear phishing messages, often built around fake job offers or business lures, that deliver a JavaScript backdoor through archive attachments or links rather than through exploits. From that foothold, operators are described as harvesting credentials from browsers, collecting email and document data, and abusing legitimate remote access or cloud services for command and control. Analysts associate the activity with espionage-style collection for financial intelligence rather than ransomware. Evidence includes suspicious archive attachments, browser credential store access, unusual logins to trading or mail platforms, and scheduled tasks added on victim hosts.

beginner.definition: Evilnum is the name for a group of attackers who target banks and online trading companies. The name is also used for some of the tools these attackers use. Their main way in is a fake email, often about a job or an invoice. The email asks you to open a file, and that file starts the attack.
beginner.whyItMatters: Financial companies hold money, client records and market plans. Losing any of these hurts customers and can break the law. This group is patient. It reads email and documents for a long time before anyone notices. If you ignore strange emails and odd login alerts, the attacker can stay for months and copy data slowly.
howItWorks: The attacker studies a company and writes an email that looks normal for that business.
A fake job offer or invoice tempts the reader to open a compressed file attached to the message.
Opening the file runs a script. A script is a short set of instructions the computer follows.
The script installs a backdoor, which is a hidden way for the attacker to control the machine.
The attacker steals saved passwords from the browser and reads mail and documents.
They hide their traffic inside normal services, such as cloud storage, so it looks routine.
beginner.example: Think of a busy airport check-in queue. A well-dressed person hands you a form that looks official and asks you to sign it. While you read the small print, a colleague of theirs walks past the desk and photographs the passenger list. The form was never real. Evilnum uses that trick on office workers. The fake job email is the form, and the quiet theft behind it is the point.
takeaways: Fake job offers and invoice messages are common first steps in targeted attacks.
Saved browser passwords are valuable, so use a password manager with strong protection.
Unusual logins on trading, mail or cloud accounts deserve a fast check.

objectives: Explain what Evilnum is and which industries its campaigns target.
Describe how a spear phishing lure leads to a JavaScript backdoor.
Describe why attackers prefer archive attachments and links over exploits.
Recognise evidence such as browser credential access and unexpected scheduled tasks.
Explain how command and control can hide inside legitimate cloud services.
Summarise why financial intelligence makes this activity an espionage concern.
